about_lead: Marble Lantern shows Java on the GPU with TornadoVM and in the browser with TeaVM. The board game is the test case.
about_what: You play against an engine that searches the game tree. When the two sides can no longer block each other, a precomputed race table chooses the move instead. The browser engine exists twice: written in C++ and compiled to WebAssembly, and written in Java and compiled to WebAssembly GC or JavaScript. All of them choose the same moves, so the benchmark compares only their speed.
about_rules: The game follows the rules of Chinese Checkers, called Sternhalma in German, for two players. Each side moves its ten pieces from one corner of the star into the opposite corner. A move is a step to a neighbouring cell or a chain of jumps over other pieces. The first side to fill the opposite corner wins. A ply is one move of one side. After 200 plies the game ends without a winner, and the side closer to its goal is ahead.
about_engines: In the offline build, everything runs in this browser: the engine, the race table and the page. The Java engine compiled to WebAssembly GC is the default; the C++ engine is the fallback. The online build adds engines that run on a server: the strongest classical player and a player with a neural network.
tech_tornadovm: Runs the neural network of the server player on the GPU, from Java.
tech_teavm: Compiles the Java engine to WebAssembly GC and to JavaScript.
tech_emscripten: Compiles the C++ engine to WebAssembly.
tech_hilla: Hilla serves the online build. React draws the page in both builds.
about_learn_lead: Five topics for developers who know Java and threads but not game AI. Each one has interactive figures with real data from this project.
about_learn_failed: The page could not be loaded. Offline before the first visit?
about_learn_architecture_teaser: One code base, three run modes: what runs in the browser, on the server and in the training jobs.
about_learn_classical_teaser: How the default engine picks a move: game tree, alpha-beta pruning, a node budget and a learned evaluation.
about_learn_inference_teaser: What the neural network computes from a board, and how Monte Carlo Tree Search uses it to choose a move.
about_learn_training_teaser: How the network learned: first from the classical engine, then from games against itself, kept only when measurably stronger.
about_learn_tuning_teaser: From settings that were simply fixed to decision rules set in advance, with the measured effect where one exists.
about_learn_glossary_teaser: Every technical term from the five topics, with a short definition, in alphabetical order.

guides_hint_eval: Marks on the board show how good each move is, and a bar shows the advantage. An engine analyses in the background for this.
guides_legend_note: Select a piece to see its targets. Pieces and targets share one scale: each move is compared with the best move of the position, so the best move shows as “top”. The badge on a piece rates the best move of that piece.
guides_note_net: A neural network plays. The marks and the advantage come from the classical engine {engine}, which runs alongside it in this browser.
guides_note_three: With three players, each mark compares a move of the player to move with the best move. The scores assume that both other players play against that player. Read the marks as a ranking of the moves, not as a chance to win.
